title: Glossary
html:
Terms are listed alphabetically. Chapter references identify relevant discussions in this book. Definitions describe the mechanisms used here, with implementation-specific limits noted where necessary.

Admission control

A decision to accept, defer, or reject work before it consumes a specified resource allocation. Admission can be enforced at an ingress, queue, or dependency boundary. Chapters 1, 4, 9, and 14.

Agent

An application-controlled loop in which model output proposes a response or tool call. Application code validates proposed actions, enforces execution limits, and records results. Chapter 13.

Arrival rate

The number of requests or operations reaching a specified boundary per unit of time. Offered arrivals, accepted work, and completed work can have different rates. Chapters 1 and 2.

At-least-once delivery

Delivery semantics that permit repeated delivery while attempting to avoid loss under the system’s documented durability, retention, and recovery conditions. Consumers need duplicate handling when repeated delivery could repeat a business effect. Chapters 3 and 12.

Authentication

Verification of a user or service identity through a trusted credential or session. A valid identity does not establish permission for an individual resource or action. Chapters 4 and 11, Appendix C.

Authorization, access control

A decision about whether a principal may perform a specific action on a particular resource under the current policy. It may depend on roles, merchant membership, resource state, or earlier approvals. Chapters 3, 4, and 11, Appendix C.

Authorization, access control

A decision about whether a principal may perform a specific action on a particular resource under the current policy. It may depend on roles, merchant membership, resource state, or earlier approvals. Chapters 3, 4, and 11, Appendix C.

Authority, state ownership

The service or record responsible for committing a business-state change and declaring its outcome. It is distinct from a caller’s permission to request that change. Chapters 3 and 11.

Authorization, payment

Provider approval that reserves or otherwise makes funds available for a payment under the provider’s contract. Capture is a separate operation. Chapters 3 and 14.

Backlog

Accepted work that has not reached its defined completion boundary. Count, age, processing rate, and work type are useful measurements. Chapters 2, 9, and 12.

Backpressure

A mechanism through which downstream capacity limits reduce upstream production or delivery. Its effect depends on whether the upstream component honors the signal. Chapter 9.

Blue-green deployment

A deployment arrangement with separate old and candidate environments. Routing can transfer requests between them. Reversing traffic also requires compatible state and sufficient destination capacity. Chapter 10.

Bounded concurrency

An enforced maximum on simultaneous operations at a specified boundary. Excess work may be rejected or admitted to a separately bounded queue. Chapters 4 and 9.

Bounded context

A boundary within which a domain model and its terminology have an agreed meaning. It informs service design without requiring a one-to-one mapping between contexts and deployable services. Chapter 11.

Bulkhead

An allocation that limits the resources one dependency or workload class can consume. A class cap prevents that class from using the entire shared allocation. A reservation additionally protects capacity for designated work. Chapters 4 and 9.

Cache-aside

A read pattern in which the application checks a cache and retrieves the authoritative value after a miss. It may then populate the cache for subsequent reads. Chapter 5.

Cache invalidation

Removal or rejection of cached data after a relevant source change. Correctness depends on covering the required writers and handling concurrent loads and delayed updates. Chapter 5.

Cache stampede

Concurrent misses that cause many callers to retrieve the same data from its source. Per-key request coalescing reduces duplicate loads, while admission limits total source work. Chapter 5.

Cache warming

Preloading selected entries before or during traffic admission. Warming itself consumes source capacity and needs a bounded workload. Chapter 5.

Canary release

Exposure of a limited customer or request population to a candidate version, followed by evaluation before further promotion. Representative per-instance demand and absolute service objectives are part of the evaluation. Chapter 10.

Cancellation

A request to stop work. Local resource release and remote execution can finish at different times, so cancelling says nothing about the outcome of a remote write. Chapters 3 and 4.

Capture

The payment operation that collects previously authorized funds, subject to the provider’s rules. Partial or repeated captures require their own operation identities. Chapters 3 and 14.

Cascading failure

Failure across service boundaries when a dependency’s delay or failure causes callers to exhaust resources or miss their own objectives. Chapters 4 and 9.

Checkpoint

Saved processing state from which execution can resume. A distributed checkpoint needs a consistent record of the required parts and evidence that they were completed. Chapters 12 and 13.

Circuit breaker

A control that suspends dependency attempts after defined failure or duration criteria are reached. Limited recovery probes determine when normal attempts may resume. Concurrency admission still applies while evidence is being collected. Chapters 4 and 9.

Cold start

The initialization period during which a process may load artifacts, open connections, or prepare execution paths. In recommendation systems, the term also describes customers or products with little interaction history. Chapters 6 and 13.

Compensation

A business operation that counteracts an earlier committed effect, such as releasing a reservation, voiding an authorization, or issuing a refund. Compensation can fail and requires its own recovery state. Chapters 3 and 14.

Component health

The measured condition of an individual service or resource. Component measurements alone cannot tell us how a complete customer operation went. Chapter 8.

Concept drift

A change in the relationship between model inputs and outcomes. Its effect on quality requires evaluation using appropriate outcome evidence. Chapter 13.

Connection-acquire time

The interval from requesting a pooled connection until acquisition or termination of the attempt. It is measured separately from connection occupancy and query execution. Chapter 1.

Connection occupancy

The interval from assigning a connection to returning it to the pool. It includes all work performed while the connection is assigned. Chapters 1 and 2.

Connection pool

A managed collection of reusable connections with a configured limit. Connections may be opened, closed, or replaced during operation. The pool limit and the acquisition-queue limit are separate controls. Chapter 1.

Configuration drift

A difference between an authoritative desired configuration revision and the revision an application or integration reports using. Detection requires both a desired revision and a trustworthy observation of the running system. Chapters 5 and 12, Appendix B.

Consumer group

In the ordinary Kafka consumer-group model used here, consumers share partition assignments, with one assigned consumer per partition during a stable assignment. Rebalances can overlap with unfinished work from an earlier assignment. Chapter 12.

Consumer lag

The difference between a partition’s relevant end position and a consumer group’s progress position. Offset distance is not always an exact record count and does not measure downstream business completion. Chapter 12.

Container image

A packaged application artifact containing filesystem layers and execution configuration. Host resources, injected configuration, and runtime behavior also affect the running application. Chapter 6.

Cycle walking

Applying a permutation over a power-of-two range again and again until the result falls inside a smaller range, so that it can serve a range that is not a power of two. Appendix B.

Data distribution drift

A change in the distribution of current inputs or customer populations relative to a reference dataset. A distribution change warrants evaluation but does not necessarily reduce model quality. Chapter 13.

Data leakage

Use of information during training or evaluation that would be unavailable for the intended production prediction. Historical availability errors are one source of leakage. Chapter 13.

Deadline

The point after which an operation should no longer continue its ordinary execution. Child calls use the available portion of the parent budget, accounting for elapsed time and required result handling. Chapters 4 and 14.

Dead-letter queue (DLQ)

A destination for records that require repair or separate handling. Durable quarantine permits progress under a defined policy, but does not complete the failed business operation. Chapter 12.

Decode

The generation stage in which an autoregressive model produces subsequent output tokens using preceding context. Chapter 13.

Distributed monolith

A description of separately deployed components that require substantial coordinated change or retain tightly coupled execution and data access. Separate deployment units alone do not make independent operation. Chapter 11.

Distributed trace

A collection of related spans describing timed work across components. Context passing, span links, sampling, and exporter reliability affect which work the trace contains. Chapter 8.

Durable log

An ordered record store whose persistence and retention are defined by its configuration and guarantees. Consumers can replay records that are still available. Chapter 12.

Embedding

A learned numerical representation used for tasks such as similarity search. The representation must be evaluated for the intended retrieval task and used with a compatible index. Chapter 13.

Epoch

A monotonically increasing identifier for successive ownership assignments. An enforcement point can reject commands from an earlier assignment by checking their epoch. Chapters 7 and 14.

Enforcement boundary

The point at which an application authorizes or refuses a protected operation. An earlier evaluation cannot replace this check when policy or input validity may have changed. Chapters 3 and 11, Appendix B.

Error budget

The amount of unsuccessful service allowed by an SLO during its measurement window, calculated using the SLI’s defined population. Chapter 8.

Error-budget burn rate

The observed bad-event fraction divided by the fraction allowed by the SLO. Relating a burn rate to elapsed-time budget consumption also requires assumptions about traffic volume. Chapter 8.

Event time

The time associated with the business event being processed. It can precede ingestion or processing by a substantial interval. Chapters 12 and 13.

Exactly-once processing

A guarantee that applies to a specified combination of input progress, state, and output. Kafka transactions can coordinate supported Kafka operations, but external effects require their own coordination or deduplication. Chapter 12.

Expand-then-contract

A migration procedure that introduces a compatible representation, transitions readers and writers, and later removes the old representation. Rollback depends on the actual compatibility of code and stored data throughout the migration. Chapter 10.

Fan-out

One request initiating several downstream operations, sequentially or concurrently. Parallel independent calls can reduce elapsed time, while still creating work at every called dependency. Chapters 1 and 2.

Fan-out on write

Copying an item into each recipient’s stored view when it is created, so that reads are cheap and writes are proportional to the audience. Very large audiences are commonly handled by pulling at read time instead. Appendix B.

Feature

An input value supplied to a model, often produced through a versioned transformation of source data. Chapter 13.

Feature contract

The definition of a feature’s meaning, units, source data, transformation, defaults, and availability or freshness rules. Chapter 13.

Feature flag

Configuration that controls execution of a code path independently of deployment. Deactivation affects subsequent execution and does not reverse earlier effects. Chapters 1 and 10.

Feature store

Storage and serving facilities for prepared model features. Correctness still depends on feature definitions, publication, historical reconstruction, and freshness. Chapter 13.

Feistel network

A construction that mixes two halves of a number over several rounds. Whatever the mixing function does, the whole construction is a permutation, so distinct inputs always give distinct outputs. Appendix B.

Fencing

Preventing a previous owner or worker from continuing an operation after authority changes. Database writes and external dispatch may require separate enforcement points. Chapters 7, 11, and 14.

Fingerprint, request

A representation, often a hash of normalized fields, used to compare the parameters defining an operation. It detects conflicting reuse of an identity and does not replace that identity. Chapter 3.

Head-of-line blocking

An ordered item prevents later work from progressing even when that later work could otherwise execute. This is narrower than general resource contention. Chapter 12.

Hidden Assumptions

The end-of-chapter review that connects a design assumption to its evidence, uncertainty, responsible owner, and decision. Chapter reviews and the worksheet use the same seven fields: scope, test condition, invariant, evidence, signal, control, and owner. Entries are revised when requirements or production measurements change. Chapters 1–14, Appendix B, and the worksheet.

Idempotency key

An identifier that allows a receiving service to recognize repeated attempts at one operation under its documented scope, concurrency, and retention rules. Responses to concurrent or unfinished attempts depend on the receiving service’s contract. Chapters 3 and 14.

Image digest

A content-addressed identifier for an image manifest or image index. An index can identify platform-specific manifests. Referencing a digest avoids depending on a mutable tag. Chapter 6.

Inference

Execution of a trained model to calculate outputs from supplied inputs. Chapter 13.

KV cache

Stored attention keys and values reused during transformer inference. Memory use depends on the architecture, representation, retained tokens, and runtime memory policy. Chapter 13.

Label

The outcome associated with a training or evaluation example. Its definition includes any observation period and attribution rules. Chapter 13.

Lease

A time-limited claim or permission. Expiry allows local authority to change under its protocol, but does not itself stop work already executing at an external service. Chapters 3 and 14.

Little’s Law

The relationship L=λWL = \lambda WL=λW, connecting average work in a defined system, its long-run flow rate, and mean time in that system. Measurements must cover the same boundary and population, with appropriate treatment of unfinished work. Chapter 2.

Liveness probe

A check used to determine whether a container should be restarted under the configured policy. A temporary dependency outage does not necessarily justify restarting the caller. Chapter 6.

Load shedding

Refusal or omission of work to limit resource demand during overload. The selected work and customer response require a documented policy. Chapter 9.

Message identity

An identifier for a particular event or message, preserved across publication attempts when consumers use it for deduplication. Chapters 3 and 12.

Model lineage

The records connecting an artifact to its training data, code, transformations, configuration, evaluation, and deployment. Chapter 13.

Negative caching

Caching an authoritative absence result for a defined period. A timeout or dependency error is never evidence of absence. Chapter 5.

Offset

A position assigned to a record in a Kafka partition. A committed consumer offset normally identifies the next position from which processing should resume. Record positions and consumer progress are distinct concepts. Chapter 12.

Operation identity

An identifier for one intended business action, preserved across its attempts and recovery. A later intentional action receives another identity even if its parameters are identical. Chapters 3, 13, and 14.

Outbox pattern

Saving an event record in the same local transaction as its associated business change, then publishing through a separate relay. Publication can be delayed or repeated. Chapters 3 and 12.

p99 latency

An estimated 99th percentile of a defined latency population. Approximately 99 percent of observations fall at or below it, subject to the measurement and quantile method. Excluded failures and timeouts can materially change its interpretation. Chapters 1 and 8.

Partition, database table

A portion of a logical table selected using a partitioning rule. Partitioning can improve management and some queries without distributing ownership across independent databases. Chapter 7.

Partition, event log

An ordered portion of a topic. In the ordinary Kafka consumer-group model, each partition has one assigned consumer during stable assignment. Internal worker concurrency requires additional progress and ordering controls. Chapter 12.

Partition key

The column or expression that assigns each row to a partition. A useful key matches the work the partitioning is meant to remove, such as archival by creation time. Chapter 7.

Partition pruning

Elimination of partitions that cannot satisfy a query’s predicates. Its effectiveness depends on the partition bounds, query expressions, and database implementation. Chapter 7.

Path health

The measured result of the complete customer-facing operation, including failures and incomplete work under the chosen definition. Chapter 8.

Point-in-time correctness

Construction of historical inputs using information available to the prediction path at the relevant time. Event time alone may be insufficient when ingestion or feature publication was delayed. Chapter 13.

Policy revision

An immutable published version of a rule set, including its precedence and validity conditions. A decision can be reproduced by identifying the revision and inputs used. Chapters 3, 5, and 12, Appendix B.

Poison record

A record that repeated execution under the current consumer implementation cannot process successfully. Repair may require data correction, code changes, or a defined quarantine procedure. Chapter 12.

Prefill

The inference stage that processes input tokens and prepares attention state before subsequent generation. Chapter 13.

Prompt caching

Provider-side reuse of the processing done for a repeated prompt prefix, which can lower the cost and latency of long shared prefixes. Hit behavior depends on the provider’s rules and on request layout, so it needs measurement. Chapter 13.

Read replica

A replicated database copy used for eligible reads. Its usefulness depends on read visibility, replication progress, capacity, and the application’s freshness requirements. Chapter 7.

Read-your-writes

A read requirement under which a client can observe its own completed writes in subsequent reads. Replica routing needs evidence that the relevant write is available. Chapter 7.

Readiness probe

A check used to determine whether a workload should receive new traffic through the applicable routing mechanism. Passing readiness does not mean every failure mode has been tested. Chapter 6.

Rate-limit identity

The identity whose allowance a request consumes, such as an IP address, API key, tenant, operation class, or the whole fleet. It decides whether one caller can exhaust an allowance shared with others. Chapter 9.

Rebalance

Reassignment of partitions among consumers. Work started under an earlier assignment may still be unfinished when a new consumer begins processing. Chapter 12.

Reconciliation

Resolution of local operation state using authoritative external evidence. It can use lookups, authenticated notifications, or repetition covered by an idempotency contract. The result may be success, failure, or continued uncertainty. Chapters 3 and 14.

RECONCILIATION_PENDING

An application state identifying an operation that requires outcome recovery. It prevents an independent replacement operation while the original effect is unresolved. Chapter 3.

Recovery-point objective (RPO)

The maximum data-loss interval or equivalent recovery point accepted by the recovery policy. Achieving it requires appropriate durability and recovery mechanisms. Chapter 14.

Recovery-time objective (RTO)

The target interval for restoring the specified service after disruption. The definition must identify what counts as restored. Chapter 14.

Replication lag

The difference between source progress and a replica’s receive, durable-storage, or replay progress. The selected stage and unit must be specified. A lag value alone cannot say whether a read is eligible for a particular write. Chapter 7.

Retry amplification

Additional dependency work caused by repeated attempts, including multiplication when several layers retry independently. Chapters 1, 2, and 4.

Retry budget

A limit on repeated attempts over a defined scope and interval. It may be expressed as a fixed allowance or a proportion of original work. Chapters 9 and 14.

Rolling deployment

Incremental replacement of application instances. Old, new, and terminating instances may coexist, affecting compatibility and aggregate resource use. Chapters 6 and 10.

Scatter-gather

Sending one logical query to several shards concurrently and combining the results. Its database work scales with request rate multiplied by the number of shards. Chapter 7.

Saga

A sequence of local transactions coordinated to complete a business operation, with compensation or other recovery for partial completion. State and operation identities support recovery between steps. Chapter 3.

Service level indicator (SLI)

A quantitative measure of a specified service result. Its definition includes the population, measurement boundary, and treatment of failed or unfinished operations. Chapter 8.

Service level objective (SLO)

A target for an SLI over a specified evaluation period. Chapter 8.

Shadow evaluation

Execution of a candidate against selected production inputs without using its output as the customer response. External effects must be disabled or isolated, and evaluation traffic needs its own resource allowance. Chapter 13.

Shard

An independently managed portion of a dataset assigned through a routing rule. Shards may have separate database resources while still sharing infrastructure and cross-shard dependencies. Chapter 7.

Shard key

The attribute that decides which shard owns a record. It determines which transactions run locally on one database and where uneven demand concentrates. Chapter 7.

Singleflight coalescing

Combining concurrent loads for one key into one source operation over a defined coordination scope. Waiters, deadlines, and cross-instance duplication still require appropriate handling. Chapter 5.

Strangler pattern

Incremental replacement of an existing implementation, transferring one caller or operation at a time to the new one while the old path serves the rest. Chapter 11.

Startup probe

A check that allows application initialization to complete before the configured readiness and liveness checks take effect. Chapter 6.

Tail sampling

Choosing which traces to retain after a request has finished, so that errors and slow requests can be retained at a higher rate than ordinary ones. Chapter 8.

Throughput

The rate of completed work at a specified boundary. It can differ from offered arrivals and from the rate of a later business effect. Chapters 2 and 12.

Time-of-check/time-of-use

A race in which a condition verified during evaluation changes before the protected operation executes. An execution-time authorization check and an authoritative revocation policy can reduce the exposure. Appendix B.

Time-to-live (TTL)

A configured lifetime after which a cache entry expires. TTL does not by itself establish source freshness, especially when an old value is inserted after a delayed read. Chapter 5.

Tombstone

A marker recording that an item was deleted, so that readers and replicas skip it before the item is physically removed. Appendix B.

Training-serving skew

A discrepancy between training inputs or transformations and those used during serving. Historical availability, defaults, joins, and feature publication can contribute. Chapter 13.

Utilization

The fraction of a defined resource allocation used over an interval. For a connection pool, average assigned connections divided by the pool limit is one such measure. Utilization alone says nothing about response latency. Chapters 1 and 2.
